author: Emma Honeybun
title: ‘The grift stops now’: Democratic midterm elections sweep brings in first Indigenous governor and senator in U.S. history
content:
The 2026 U.S. midterms resulted in several firsts, including the victories of Peggy Flanagan and Deb Haaland, the first Indigenous women to serve as state senator and governor, respectively, in the country’s history.


“My ancestors came to the Rio Grande Valley in the late 1200s, and this beautiful land has sustained all of us for generations,” Haaland said in her victory speech Tuesday night. “Just off this road, my grandmother was taken to boarding school, and along with my grandfather, survived through a time when the federal government attempted to strip them of their languages, traditions and identities. Yet, we are still here.”


Although the results have not been finalized, the Democrats have been favoured to win the U.S. House of Representatives (236 seats to 129) and Senate (54 to 44), a sweeping result which flipped 29 seats from red to blue, as of Wednesday afternoon.


Midterm elections are held two years after a presidential election. All members of Congress, also called the House of Representatives, are up for election, and 33 of the Senate’s 100 seats were up for grabs.


Alongside Flanagan (Minnesota) and Haaland (New Mexico), the midterms also brought in Abdul El-Sayed, the first Muslim senator in Michigan; Chris Pappas, the first openly gay senator in New Hampshire; and Keisha Lance Bottoms, the first Black female governor in Georgia.


The Associated Press (AP) reported that the win for blue was the result of “a revolt against President Donald Trump’s policies,” including the tariff war with Canada and the ongoing war with Iran.


Twice as many voters wanted to “express opposition” to Trump, compared to those who wanted to support him, according to results from an AP national poll, which resulted in Democrats gaining control of historically red states such as Texas and South Carolina.


Democrats are “ready to launch a 100-day agenda to lower the costs of gas, groceries and healthcare and conduct vast oversight and investigations into Trump and his administration, with impeachment an option,” the AP continued.


In a 25-minute victory speech, Flanagan said, “no more ballrooms, no more bombs and tax breaks for billionaires … The grift stops now.”


Flanagan was one of several populist candidates in the 2026 midterms, with a campaign that “did not represent billionaires,” she said, and supported Treaty rights.


Flanagan, who is Ojibwe, won with a 10 per cent lead. Although she is the first Indigenous woman in the Senate, she isn’t new to politics — she was elected as the state’s lieutenant governor in 2018 and served in the Minnesota House of Representatives from 2015 to 2019.


She was also the first woman of colour to be elected to statewide office in Minnesota, according to the Center for American Women and Politics, and was the highest-ranked Indigenous official in the country at the time of her 2018 win.


“The name you voted on the ballot says Peggy Flanagan, but my Ojibwe name speaks in a loud and clear voice,” she said. “You helped a small and scrappy, often underestimated enrolled member of the White Earth Nation become the first Native American woman in history to be elected to the U.S. Senate.”


Flanagan is credited as the driving force behind

Minnesota’s Missing and Murdered Indigenous Relatives office

, the first state-wide office of its kind in the country.


She was also a vocal advocate when it came to passing the

Minnesota Indian Family Preservation Act

, a law which notifies Indigenous American governments when a child enters the welfare system, as well as strengthens family protection for Indigenous Peoples, in 2023.


It’s Indigenous Peoples Day in Minnesota – an opportunity to embrace the power, beauty, and richness of our community.


We are resilient, we are still here, and we will always be here in Mni Sota Makoce.

pic.twitter.com/uMZCdGb3Te


— Lt. Governor Peggy Flanagan (@LtGovFlanagan)

October 12, 2026

In her speech, she thanked Walz for his “historic work to strengthen tribal-state relations.”


“To all the young people out there who look like me, to the daughters and to the sons who too often are forgotten or erased, I see you,” she said. “Do not be disheartened that it took 250 years for one of us to get here, be inspired by the fact that with grit and …

author: Sharon Zhang
title: Angie Nixon Hints at Another Senate Run in 2028, After Being Heavily Outspent
content:
Nixon, Democrats’ candidate for US Senate in Florida, didn’t receive any funding from the party’s Senate PACs.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

Democratic candidate Angie Nixon has suggested she could run again in 2028 after being narrowly defeated in her race for U.S. Senate in Florida on Tuesday, falling to Republican opponent Ashley Moody by roughly 3 points after being massively outspent in the race written off by the Democratic establishment.

Moody received 50.9 percent of the vote to Nixon’s 48 percent, still overcoming a 10-point swing toward Democrats compared to 2024. Nixon got roughly the same proportion of the vote as Florida governor candidate David Jolly, a former Republican member of the House who left that party in 2018 and registered as a Democrat last year.

The race was a special election to fill the Senate seat left vacant by Marco Rubio, who won the seat in 2022 but left to become Secretary of State. Moody was chosen by Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis as a temporary replacement, and has now been officially elected to serve the rest of the term.

This means that the seat will be up for grabs again in 2028 — and Nixon, who has already defied the odds in her race, has left the door open for another run.

In her concession speech on Tuesday, Nixon struck a positive tone despite the loss, touting the movement built by her campaign. “When we started this campaign, people told us it could not be done,” she said. “They told us we couldn’t compete with the political establishment.”

“I need y’all to stay in this fight. The war is not over. 2028 is around the corner. So Ashley Moody, you better get it right. Cause we’re coming for you,” Nixon said. Let’s go win y’all.”

Indeed, it is extraordinary that a member of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) could come so close to a win in the red state. Though Nixon has rejected the socialist label, the DSA has been relentlessly vilified by conservatives and liberals alike, and Nixon has embraced left-wing stances like rejecting assistance to Israel and supporting Medicare for All.

Nixon’s primary race was already historic. She won despite being outspent by roughly 13 to 1, and raised just under $1 million compared to $16 million raised by opponent Alex Vindman, a former national security official in Donald Trump’s first administration.

The Democratic establishment, however, seemingly wrote off her race — or potentially actively opposed her bid. Neither the Senate Majority PAC nor the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC) spent any money supporting Nixon’s race, The American Prospect points out.

According to AdImpact data, Republicans spent $28.7 million on TV ads supporting Moody, while Democrats only spent $7.9 million. Nixon’s campaign says that support and fundraising from Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont) was an enormous help.

“Bernie’s impact on our campaign was immeasurable. He was one of our most important partners, by far,” said Kevin Lata, Nixon’s deputy campaign manager, on X on Tuesday evening. “I can almost guarantee that the democrats who are blaming Bernie did very little themselves to help, and should instead be looking inward, not at him.”

Some politicians chalked the lack of support from the main arms of the Democratic Party as racism as well as pro-centrist bias. Last month, Rep. Ayanna Pressley (D-Massachusetts) called out the DSCC for this disparity.

“It is shameful that we are not seeing an equitable investment in progressive and diverse candidates like Abdul El-Sayed, like Angie Nixon, like Scott Colom,” said Pressley. Nixon and Colom, whose Senate race in Mississippi is too close to call as of Wednesday afternoon, are Black, while progressive Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed is Arab American.

“They have earned and need the investment so that we can have a majority,” Pressley said, as Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-New York) nodded beside her.

Nixon added on Wednesday, after sweeping Democratic wins even across traditionally red states in the South, that Democrats must not write off the region.

“Invest In The South,” Nixon wrote.

author: Lilli Akpaleeapik
title: Tuberculosis documentary shows healing through sharing stories
content:
Iqaluit’s Astro Theatre was filled with people Tuesday evening for the première of a documentary that follows a group of tuberculosis survivors and youth as they find closure over their forced relocations decades ago.


Between the 1940s-1960s, the federal government transported thousands of Inuit to southern sanatoriums for tuberculosis treatment without their consent or without informing them about what was happening.


Many Inuit never returned home.


Taqqut Productions joined hands with The SeeChange Initiative to create

Our Elders are so Important to Us: A Tuberculosis Sanatorium Healing Journey

, a 29-minute documentary that follows youth and survivors as they connect over these relocations, in an effort to provide healing and closure.


“If we value our elders as much as we say we do as Inuit, why not listen to their stories,” asked Naomi Tatty, the intercultural health lead at SeeChange, a non-profit and one of the leads for the documentary.


“Why not put their words out there and help us younger generations, and the generations ahead of us, understand what our families went through?”


She was on site for the screening and to help facilitate discussion afterwards, at the Storehouse.


Tuberculosis is an airborne bacterial disease characterized by a cough, weight loss, night sweats, and a fever. Without treatment, it can cause serious complications and death.


In 2025, a group of TB survivors who had been relocated while sick, alongside others who were affected by the relocation of family members, made a journey to the former Mountain Sanatorium site in Hamilton, Ont. While there, they shared their history with youth and discussed how tuberculosis continues to affect people to this day.


Astro Theatre was filled with survivors, youth, health-care workers and community members to view the film and participate in the discussion afterward.


The idea for the healing journey was sparked by former prime minister Justin Trudeau’s 2019

apology

 over TB sanatoriums, and his subsequent announcement of the The Nanilavut Initiative, a collaborative project that helps Inuit locate family members who never came home.


Tatty told Nunatsiaq News that her mother, or anaana, Ida Atagoyuk, was a TB survivor who spent three and a half years alone in treatment. She was present when the apology was given. But she wondered, Tatty said, what else was being done for healing. The 2025 healing journey was a product of that question, and the documentary followed.


Tatty also highlighted the importance of youth for facilitating healing how important it is to share stories.


“Hopefully there’s a ripple effect of the younger generation to be able to have a mindset of understanding and to gain that knowledge and more understanding towards their upbringing and their homes,” she said to Nunatsiaq News.


Tuberculosis is still a crisis within Inuit Nunangat, and Nunavut has the highest rate of active tuberculosis of any province or territory in Canada.


So far this year, there have been 32 tuberculosis cases reported in seven communities.

author: William D. Hartung
title: The Democrats have a mandate for peace — here are 4 urgent priorities
content:
This article

The Democrats have a mandate for peace — here are 4 urgent priorities

 was originally published by

Waging Nonviolence

.


Voters in the midterm elections dealt a decisive blow to Trump’s war agenda and have created new possibilities for challenging militarism and ending the debacle in Iran. The blue tsunami that swept across the country was driven by

many issues

, including tariffs, corruption and higher prices, but voter discontent was rooted in opposition to the war against Iran and the high fuel costs and inflation that resulted. 


The election outcome presents an opportunity for activists to intensify pressures to end the war, reverse excessive arms spending, restore necessary funding for vital social and environmental priorities, and protect democracy. We need to elect a government that will build the foundations for a forward-looking, progressive foreign policy by expanding essential diplomatic capabilities and restoring U.S. support for global cooperation.


The current electoral realignment can be compared to the dramatic political transformation that occurred in the 2006 midterm elections. That year, the Iraq war was the

decisive issue

 in helping Democrats pick up 31 seats in the U.S. House of Representatives and six in the Senate. Then as now, affordability and immigration were important issues, but the dominant concern was war in the Middle East. As analysts argued at the time, Iraq was the “

Archimedean lever

” that shifted voters toward Democrats. 


But when the new Congress assembled in 2007, Democratic Party leaders equivocated. Speaker of the House Nancy Pelosi and Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid proposed a legislative agenda for the new Congress that ignored Iraq. 


Embed from Getty Images


As Tom Hayden wrote in  “Ending the War in Iraq”, antiwar activists were furious. Constituents bombarded Democratic leaders with demands to prioritize withdrawal from Iraq. Protesters gathered outside Pelosi’s San Francisco home. An estimated 100,000 people marched in an antiwar rally in Washington, D.C. 


Democratic leaders quickly got the message and agreed on a legislative strategy to establish a timetable for withdrawal, which Congress subsequently adopted. 


We may need to exert similar pressures now to ensure that the new Congress fulfills its political mandate to end the Iran war and takes action to reverse other elements of Trump’s dangerous foreign policies. 


The threats to peace have grown significantly in recent years, and they are enormous and multifaceted. An unending, illegal war in Iran and related carnage throughout the Middle East; the arming of repressive regimes, up to and including enabling genocide in Gaza and occupation and ethnic cleansing in Lebanon; the skyrocketing of military-related spending (proposed at more than

$1.5 trillion

 this year) and an accelerating nuclear arms race. All of this is occurring while the Pentagon is

moving

 rapidly towards the deployment of AI-driven weapons systems that can operate without human pilots or human control.


Sign Up for our Newsletter


We’ll send you a weekly email with the latest articles.


The threat or use of force has taken precedence over diplomacy, economic development and peacebuilding programs. The White House has rebuked democratic allies in Canada and Europe while coddling authoritarian regimes in Russia and Saudi Arabia. 


The human, economic and environmental consequences of these militarist policies have been disastrous —

trillions

 of dollars wasted,

hundreds of thousands

 of lives lost and

tens of millions

 of people driven from their homes.      


The pursuit of peace abroad depends on the defense of democracy at home. Legislators must protect democracy by removing obstacles to the exercise of basic rights, including the right to vote, the right of assembly, freedom of speech and an end to discrimination based on race, gender, religion and sexual preference. We need to create an America where every person is cherished, and every person is treated with the dignity they deserve — and then we need to extend that ethos to the rest of the world.


For cooperation, not confrontation


On the foreign policy front, we must demand congressional and executive action on the following major goals:

: Prohibit the use of funds for military hostilities over, in, or off the shores of Iran. Work through the United Nations to reach a comprehensive diplomatic agreement to open …

author: Chad Nelson
title: La Guerra dei Politici contro gli Immigrati è un Diversivo
content:
Di

Chad Nelson

. Originale.

The Political Class’s War on Immigrants is a Diversion

, del 30 gennaio 2015. Traduzione italiana di

Enrico Sanna

.


Al dibattito sulla nomina a ministro della giustizia di Loretta Lynch, il 28 gennaio scorso, i repubblicani erano ansiosi di chiederle fino a che punto avrebbe spinto la sua politica amica di quella categoria di persone che il governo definisce “immigrati clandestini”. In un

confronto di idee

,

Jeff Sessions

, repubblicano, severo in materia di immigrazione, chiedeva chi, secondo la Lynch, ha il diritto di lavorare in America. In particolare, chi ne ha “più diritto”: un immigrato in regola, un cittadino o qualcuno entrato illegalmente nel paese? La Lynch ha saggiamente ignorato le tre ipotesi e ha risposto che vorrebbe che tra i lavoratori americani ci fosse anche chi non ha documenti.


Il modo di porre la domanda di Sessions, e le risposte implicitamente suggerite, dicono molto sul modo di pensare distorto della classe politica. Secondo il pensiero antiimmigrazione bipartitico, il Congresso avrebbe, come nota Sheldon Richman, “il diritto di concedere il permesso di lavorare”. Cosa che purtroppo è diventata legge comune. Oggi, chi ha diritto ad un posto di lavoro lo decidono perlopiù i burocrati di Washington e gli interessi particolari che si giocano così il diritto di

vendere

 i loro servizi in monopolio. Tu pensi di essere libero di svolgere un lavoro che hai scelto, in realtà gli innumerevoli requisiti imposti dallo stato limitano drasticamente quella tua scelta. E se sei abbastanza fortunato da superare tutti gli ostacoli, la possibilità di mantenere l’attività è spesso impedita dalla palude normativa.


I politici confidano in questo enorme potere per tenere al giogo i loro soggetti. Il diritto di dare un lavoro, con tutti gli annessi e connessi che accompagnano il potere di offrire un privilegio, permette alla classe politica di arricchirsi nel modo più efficiente possibile. Quando il lavoro, che si tratti di immigrati irregolari o afroamericani, diventa lavoro in nero, i politici perdono la capacità di intercettarlo e estorcere tributo. Non rispettare quell’intrico fatto di tasse e norme amministrative e professionali, per non dire del sistema di licenze che imbriglia intere professioni, può significare la fame. Si tratta di una struttura falsamente fatta passare per protezione di produttori e consumatori.


I burocrati non temono l’immigrazione clandestina. Temono l’impossibilità di sfruttare il lavoro degli immigrati irregolari. Sessions e gli altri come lui al Congresso nascondono le loro paure dietro la retorica del “noi contro loro”, in un’astuta messinscena al servizio di importanti fini politici. Con questo trucchetto i politici vogliono far credere di essere preoccupati non per la perdita del loro guadagno personale, ma per il “vostro” posto di lavoro, la “vostra” sanità, la “vostra” pensione. A chi è in norma (e paga le tasse) dicono che sta svolgendo un compito patriottico. Non bisogna odiare la scrematura dei loro stipendi, al contrario c’è da esserne fieri perché così si contribuisce al benessere generale. Il nemico è chi lavora senza permesso, chi distrugge il nobile impiego di chi è in norma. “Voi” siete i buoni e “loro” i cattivi. Gli immigrati senza documenti, politicamente impotenti, sono un facile bersaglio di Washington, servono a nascondere la finta isteria dei politici dietro una maschera umanitaria come neanche la peggiore agenzia pubblicitaria potrebbe fare.


Questa isteria, è bene dirlo, è rivolta a: 1) i disoccupati e i precari americani e 2) i pensionati. Il “noi contro loro” si rafforza quando ti dicono che se non si ferma l’immigrazione puoi perdere qualcosa. Chi ha un buon lavoro sicuro ed è relativamente indipendente dallo stato ha poche ragioni per preoccuparsi per qualcosa che riguarda il lavoro e i meccanismi retributivi altrui. Sono i vecchi, molti dei quali immigrati o discendenti di immigrati, che generalmente sono poco tolleranti verso la nuova ondata migratoria dal sud. Questa alterizzazione fa facile presa sui vecchi, i quali difficilmente conoscono gli immigrati e finiscono per credere che la loro presenza porta alla disintegrazione della cultura americana.


È lo stato, vera fonte di insicurezza e rovina culturale, a derubare i lavoratori e le persone oneste. Sondare le ragioni dietro l’interesse dei politici per l’immigrazione, svelarne i veri motivi, e allo stesso tempo riconoscere l’umanità dei nostri …

author: Santana Dreaver
title: After decades of suppression, poll suggests ‘Canadians’ are embracing Indigenous cultural burns
content:
Cultural burns have been suppressed all over the world. Thanks to Indigenous firekeepers, Canadians are changing their minds. Photo: Amy Cardinal Christianson


This article has been co-published

with The Narwhal

 as part of their 

2026 Indigenous journalism fellowship

.


Generations of Indigenous fire stewards have long advocated for their knowledge to be respected as science, in “B.C.” and across “Canada.” And now, a national poll suggests “Canadians” agree Indigenous-led fire management is critical for the future. 


The poll, conducted by Pollara Strategic, says “Canadians” are starting to learn more about what Indigenous fire stewardship means, shifting public opinion in support of it.


According to the 

Indigenous Leadership Initiative

 data released in September, 49 per cent of those surveyed had never heard of Indigenous fire stewardship before, but once it was described, 84 per cent said it is important for “Canada.”


The poll, which surveyed 2,250 “Canadians” in August, found that 76 per cent support First Nations cultural burning. For Sheri Lysons, that finding is long overdue. 


“It’s about time,” she said.


Lysons is Secwépemc from the Adams Lake Indian Band, located in “B.C.’s” Southern Interior, and has decades of experience fighting and stewarding fire. 


Lysons says that non-Indigenous people are changing their minds about practices such as cultural burns, “because they’ve seen the benefits of it.”


Reflecting on “B.C.” provincial legislation amendments made two years ago to support cultural burning, she says Indigenous firekeepers are doing “the work that needs to be done.”


“There’s so much misinformation out there,” she says. 


Sheri Lysons is a former fire deputy chief in her nation. She comes from a firefighting family. Photo: Supplied by Sheri Lysons


Lysons says education about cultural burns helps remove stigma, and with wildfires becoming more rampant, people are becoming more open to different preparedness methods.


As for the 82 per cent of “Canadians” in support of federal Indigenous fire stewardship funding, Lysons wants to see that number reach 100 per cent.


Indigenous firekeepers surprised by the statistics


Fire has been used by Indigenous people for countless generations as an ancestral land management and ceremonial practice. 


But today, a campfire is as close as some Indigenous people get to it, which is by government design. For more than a century, 

colonial policies

 disrupted and outlawed the practice of cultural burning, viewing fire as a threat and something to immediately suppress.


For those who come from families who managed to keep the tradition of cultural burns going, many wait year-round for the opportunity to hit the land with their torches.


While it is serious business, burning days are days when families and the community come together and spend time on the land. 


Cultural burns typically happen in the spring and late fall. Photo: Supplied by Amy Cardinal Christianson


The jokes about which uncle or auntie are going to let the fire get away from them, the stories shared between generations and the smells and crackling sounds of the burn create memories which last a lifetime.


Tiffany Traverse is Secwépemc and has more than a decade of experience working in the fire industry. 


She’s held various positions with the BC Wildfire Service and currently has a board position with the Salish Firekeepers Society, a non-profit organization committed to promoting and revitalizing cultural burns in Interior “B.C.”


“When I was drilling down into the particulars about that poll, it was really nice to see that people are changing their opinions … on what cultural fire means and how important it is,” she says.  


“I was really pleasantly surprised to see that.”


Tiffany Traverse is a seed and land steward at Fourth Sister Farm. She says she is “pleasantly surprised” to see people are changing their opinions on Indigenous fire practices. Photo: Supplied by Shelanne Justice


She says education is key to those statistics, having started her career at a time when Indigenous fire stewardship practices were less supported.


“A percentage of people didn’t know about cultural fire and once they were educated on that, their opinion on it changed,” she says.


“I thought it was really refreshing to see, especially with all of the anti-Indigenous racism that we’ve been seeing.” 


It’s a sentiment shared by Nlaka’pamux firefighter George Campbell, who …

author: Kiara Green
title: What Rights Are at Stake in the Supreme Court’s 2026-27 Term?
content:
The US Supreme Court reconvened on October 5 for its 2026-27 term which concludes in June of 2027. Cases involving the rights of immigrants, rules governing elections, LGBTQIA rights, and more, stand at the forefront this term. The Court’s decisions could have significant consequences for how federal and state laws protect individual rights.

The Court begins this term with a 6–3 conservative majority. Three of the nine justices, Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh, and Amy Coney Barrett, were nominated by President Donald Trump. Recent decisions, including the overturning of Dobbs and rulings affecting the enforcement of the Voting Rights Act, have already reshaped the legal landscape. This term, the justices will consider additional disputes over voting regulations and the rights of young people.

Among these cases is Republican National Committee v. Mi Familia Vota, which is scheduled to be heard on December 8. The Court will decide whether Arizona can require proof of citizenship to register to vote and if the National Voter Registration Act prohibits Arizona from canceling the registrations of non-citizens within 90 days of a federal election.

Despite the lack of evidence of noncitizen voting, concerns about voter eligibility have led to policies that can create additional hurdles for eligible voters in Arizona, especially indigenous people. Arizona is home to one of the largest Indigenous reservations in the US, but was one of the last states to allow Indigenous people to vote.

Indigenous votes play a vital role in deciding the outcome of state and federal elections. In 2020, Indigenous voters from the Hopi and Navajo reservation cast nearly 60,000 votes.

The Supreme Court’s decision could affect how Arizona and other states administer voter registration and verify citizenship. It will also determine how federal law limits states’ authority to change voter registration records close to an election.

The Court will also hear International Partners for Ethical Care, Inc. v. Ferguson on December 7. The Administration has vilified the queer community spewing anti-trans and homophobic rhetoric in the name of religious freedom. The decision of this case will impact the livelihood of queer adolescents that struggle with their gender identity.

The case is challenging a Washington State law on whether runaway minors can seek access to gender-affirming care without parental permission. Ending gender-affirming care has been a top priority for the Trump administration pushing for hospitals to discriminate against patients based on gender orientation and identity. This pressure has led at least six hospitals to agree to refuse gender-affirming hormones and surgery for transgender young people and agreed to make payments to the federal government.

As the term continues, the Court’s decisions will shape how federal protections and state laws apply to voting access, family rights and LGBTQIA+ communities. Oral arguments will offer insight into the justices’ questions, but final rulings are expected later in the term.

The Supreme Court’s work affects people across the country, often in ways that reach beyond the specific parties involved in a case. As the midterm elections approach on November 3, make a plan to vote, bring friends, spread the word. For nonpartisan voter registration information, election dates and voting resources, visit Vote411.org/feminist.

author: Victoria Valenzuela
title: Incarcerated Los Angeles Youth Fought for the Right to Hug Their Parents — and Won
content:
This story was co-published with


Truthout

.


Mercedes Maradiaga sat across from her 19-year-old son in the Los Padrinos Juvenile Hall in Los Angeles in complete devastation. Her son had at that point been incarcerated at the prison for two years and she had visited him every weekend. But that day in September 2024 was especially hard because it was their first visit since he had been beaten by officers earlier that week in a space in the jail where there were no cameras. The guards had jumped on and kicked him, and he needed surgery for a torn ACL. All she wanted was to give him a hug and reassure him that she was there. However, because of the no-contact visit policies at Los Padrinos, she was unable to give him that comfort.


Even during birthdays and holidays, they weren’t allowed to embrace. The boy endured the jail’s horrible living conditions — including rat infestations and flooded toilets — but couldn’t hug his mom for a moment of escape.


“I couldn’t even let him know I’m here just with the little hug,” Maradiaga said. “It would have meant everything to him. It was sad, and I did that for four years.”


Los Padrinos had

reopened a year earlier

 in 2023, after being shut down in 2019 due to conditions that violated the Board of State and Community Corrections (BSCC) standards, including abuses by staff. Six officers were criminally charged with

assault and child abuse

 for using pepper spray on several teenage girls. Reports

also cited a decreasing youth population

 as a factor for closure, yet staff

claimed to feel “outnumbered.”

 When Los Padrinos closed, youth were shuffled to another facility called Central Juvenile Hall — and then in 2023, that facility was closed down due to similar issues. Los Padrinos reopened, and just months later, the abuses restarted. In 2025,

30 officers were criminally charged

 by the California Attorney General with child endangerment and abuse, conspiracy, and battery for encouraging “gladiator fights” that pit youth against each other.


Olivia Shields, a justice transformation policy coordinator at Urban Peace Institute, described the constant closing and reopening of BSCC facilities as a “cycle of noncompliance.” Shields said the Los Angeles County Probation Department has ultimately failed with these maneuvers to address the core issue: unmet youth needs — which won’t be addressed through incarceration but through coordinated care in the form of individualized, robust support systems and resources.


“Rather than decarcerate these populations of young people and find community-based alternatives or step-downs for as many of them as possible, they basically shift the youth around from facility to facility to avoid noncompliance,” Shields said.


Long before the closing of Los Padrinos in 2019, the facility had a bad reputation among Angelenos. Maradiaga recalled hearing disturbing stories about the facility in the ’80s when she was a kid.


“I think it needs to be shut down,” Maradiaga said. “I think that there needs to be a better way for the youth. I don’t think locking them away from their family is the answer.”


The Appeal in Your Inbox


Subscribe to our newsletters for regular updates, analysis and context straight to your email.


          Sign Up


Barred From Basic Human Contact


When Ilana Parach, executive director and co-founder of

Hoops 4 Justice

, went inside Los Padrinos with a basketball and mentorship program, she quickly learned about what youth were facing inside. She felt it was important to give them a platform to express their needs directly, so she pivoted to working with them on legislation.


“They made a list of specific programs they wanted — resources for their families, reentry support,” Parach said. “At the bottom of that list, they wrote, ‘We want to hug our moms.’”


Incarcerated youth directly told her that one parent who hugged her son during a visit on his birthday then had her visit terminated and future visits suspended for two weeks. She said another youth was incarcerated for three years and had no choice but to watch his mother cry during the visits because she couldn’t hug him.


Contact visitation policies vary across California and are often left at the discretion of correctional officers. Parach said youth and staff both told her that Los Padrinos stopped allowing contact visits after the pandemic. Parach said that during meetings of the board of supervisors, she heard officers citing staffing shortages …

title: In the Crosshairs of the Far-Right Advance : An Update on Anti-Fascists and Anarchists in Greece
content:
Anarchist graffiti from Athens, Greece (2026)


The anarchist movement in Greece faces a new wave of repression. Urged on by the US and its obsession with combatting “far-left extremism,” the Greek state has targeted anti-authoritarians with new legal charges and attacked demonstrations, while fascists carry out street attacks and plot their return to the halls of power. Amidst a landscape of ongoing austerity, terrorism designations, lethal prisons, and ferocious wildfires, anarchists nonetheless continue to forge a combative culture of revolutionary solidarity.


In this article, we present an interview with an anarchist comrade in Athens assessing the current situation among anarchists and anti-fascists in Greece, along with analysis of the US’s role in advancing state repression and fantasies of Western supremacy.


The US and Greece: A Right-Wing Alliance to Defend “The West”


Earlier this month, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio delivered a speech at the Pnyx in Athens. With the historic Acropolis and the Parthenon—that ancient symbol of Western democracy, constructed with slave labor—in the background, he delivered a warning message to Greece’s political and business elite.


“The course we take will determine whether the West maintains its place at the head of the world or resigns itself to a future of atrophy and servitude and decline,” Rubio cautioned. “We will either choose to act now or lose the choice to act at all.” Lamenting how “nationalism became a dirty word,” he called for renewed militarism, praised Christian faith and martyrdom, and announced a new counterterrorism information-sharing program between the two countries. His statements were calculated to reinforce the colonial legacy of Western dominance over the rest of the world, while urging the worst of Greek society to imitate America’s current political trajectory.


US Secretary of State Marco Rubio constructs an elaborate photo op for his defense of nationalism, militarism, and “the West” (October 7, 2026).


The speech came in the wake of a conference Rubio convened in July that aimed to coordinate intensified repression against “far-left extremism.” The following month, the US government imposed a “global terrorist” designation on the Italy-based

Autistici/Inventati (A/I) tech collective

, which operated the free publishing platform NoBlogs.org.


Greece’s right-wing politicians and business leaders benefiting from the country’s endless austerity measures are heeding Rubio’s call to preserve the hubris of the so-called West. Meanwhile, governments are collaborating to escalate repression against any truly revolutionary movements that challenge the world’s current status quo.


Greece’s strategic importance to Western powers is rooted in its symbolic status as the birthplace of “Western Civilization,” as well as its strategic location in the world today. The country offers the US access to four military sites, including a dedicated Navy base in Crete’s Souda Bay. Those with a longer memory have not forgotten how the US supplied napalm to Greece’s fascist forces, who worked with the Nazis during World War II and later with the British and US in a Cold War anti-communist alliance. Fascists dropped American napalm on Greek partisan resistance fighters during the civil war from 1946 to 1949, scorching bodies and charring forests, leaving the countryside scarred to this day.


More recently, the Greek people were pummeled by the 2008 global economic crisis, brought on in part by Wall Street firms such as Goldman Sachs that raked in immense profits while destabilizing the world’s economy and immiserating millions. The US then contributed to the austerity measures imposed on Greece in 2010 by the International Monetary Fund (IMF), leading to years of ferocious resistance to neoliberal capitalism and government complicity.


Today, Greece’s current New Democracy regime upholds

the legacy of the brutal military junta

 of 1967-1974, promoting the image of Greece as a symbol European supremacy as invoked by Rubio. Despite its nationalist rhetoric, the government continues to lick the boots of the US, crushing opposition in the streets and enforcing a never-ending precarity on the majority of Greece’s increasingly exhausted and numb population.

title: Rising from the Ashes : The Yellow Vests Return as France Burns
content:
Helicopter hovering over Place de la République during the curfew implemented in Paris.


Over the past month, France has erupted in a nationwide rebellion that has shaken the ruling order to its core. As politicians of all stripes focus on polishing their brand image for the next

presidential election

 in May 2027, high school students have

organized

 on a grassroots level. Through occupations, blockades, and street protests, they have taken a stand against both the deplorable conditions of their schools today and the

menacing future

 that looms ahead of them. They took France and the entire world by surprise with their determined mass resistance and their courage in confronting the police forces sent to repress them.


After weeks of daily actions and nationwide demonstrations, leading to an unprecedented wave of arrests targeting rebellious youth, the Macron government was reaching a political impasse. It desperately tried to buy time by opening dialogue with some student organizations, in hopes of blunting the force of the movement until the upcoming school break slowed its momentum.


However, the authorities had not anticipated several developments. First, the students multiplied their force by joining the national call to take the streets on Saturday, October 17 to reignite the

Yellow Vests movement

, the popular mobilization against high gas prices and government austerity policies that emerged in 2018. Second, anger over the intense police violence of the previous weeks drew even more people in the streets. Third and most dramatically, the day’s protests snowballed into an insurrectionary situation that

surpassed

 what we experienced eight years ago during the height of the Yellow Vests struggle.


This new wave of collective rage that swept over the cities of France last week has plunged the current government into a deeper crisis. Politicians scrambled to capitalize on the upheavals, while authorities responded by implementing more authoritarian policies on a national scale. In the following article, we describe how the dramatic events around October 17 unfolded, analyzing their significance and reflecting on what is at stake.


Burning barricades blocking a narrow street in the historical part of downtown Bordeaux (October 17.)


Glowing Embers of Discontent


In 2018, the Yellow Vest movement emerged into the French political landscape seemingly out of nowhere. This grassroots wave of protests formed a reaction against rising gas prices and worsening living conditions among the country’s lower and middle classes. After decades of economic crises, inflation, and harsh neoliberal austerity policies, a portion of the population was feeling isolated, disenfranchised, and abandoned. The capitalist dream of ease and opulence that successive governments had promoted was turning into a living nightmare for a growing number of individuals. The politically diverse movement, named after the fluorescent emergency vests drivers were required to carry in their vehicles, made visible the ongoing economic emergency that gripped more and more people across France.


Due to its open-ended form, the Yellow Vests initially attracted populists from the left and the right and autonomous participants with a range of grievances against the ruling order. From the beginning, an internal struggle unfolded within the movement as radical participants

confronted

 far-right and fascist factions and attempted to prevent cooptation by reactionaries. Over time, the Yellow Vest movement gradually shifted to embrace more anti-capitalist and anti-state perspectives.


Since the initial wave of Yellow Vest protests died down in 2020, the economic situation in France has worsened. The gap between rich and poor has continued to

widen

, while the Macron government accelerated its dismantling of public services. International conflicts from Ukraine to Iran have further impacted the French economy, worsening inflation and driving up prices on essential goods, energy, and gas.


It is no surprise that people facing such economic pressure would take to the streets to express their discontent. And what better way to threaten the current ruling order than to bring the Yellow Vest movement back from the dead?


It is difficult to know the exact source of this proposal, which began to spread on social media platforms such as Tik Tok and Instagram in September and rapidly went viral. However, veterans from the Yellow Vest struggle along …

author: anred
title: Perdió Trump y los demócratas recuperan el control de las Cámaras: velorio en la Casa Rosada
content:
Los demócratas dominarán el próximo Congreso. Consiguieron triunfos en estados en disputa como los de Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Carolina del Norte, Ohio, Carolina del Sur y Texas, que le permitirán controlar el Senado. La votación general donde superan a los republicanos por más de diez puntos le permitirán obtener una amplia mayoría que se expresará en la Cámara de Representantes (Diputados), que se renueva por completo. La derrota de Trump ha sido un golpe muy fuerte para el gobierno argentino, que se ató a su destino político, y que fue correspondido por el gobierno estadounidense con apoyos políticos y financieros en momentos clave.

Por Guillermo Cieza, para Huella del Sur.


En el Senado, según los últimos conteos, los demócratas habrían obtenido 54 curules y los republicanos apenas retienen 44. En la Cámara de Diputados la diferencia será aún más aplastante. Los demócratas obtendrían 231 representantes, contra 139 de los republicanos.


El deterioro económico de la mayoría de la población estadounidense y sus promesas incumplidas de acabar con las guerras, bajar el precio de los combustibles y publicar el archivo Epstein, parecen haber sido decisivas en estas elecciones. La marea azul (demócrata) parece haberse asentado en el fuerte apoyo del voto latino (una comunidad asediada por las deportaciones), en el cambio de voto de los jóvenes y en la ruptura de sectores rurales con la gestión (por razones económicas y morales).


Gina Hinojosa será la primera latina en gobernar Texas, un estado de fuerte ascendencia republicana. Lo mismo sucederá en California donde se impuso Xavier Becerra, por amplio margen. Otra de las sorpresas fue el triunfo de Abdul El Sayed que ganó en Michigan y se convirtió en el primer senador musulmán de EEUU.


También hay un crecimiento del ala izquierda del Partido demócrata. Janeese Lewis George, miembro del partido Socialista Democrático de América (DSA) ganó las elecciones a la alcaldía de Washington DC, la capital del país. El resultado fue abrumador. La candidata socialista democrática obtuvo el 84% contra su rival republicana, Rhonda Hamilton, que obtuvo el 10,3%.


La derrota del gobierno republicano que se estima en una cifra no inferior a 10 puntos, y la pérdida del Congreso, coloca al presidente Trump en una situación muy complicada, por las dificultades legislativas que tendrá en el futuro y porque estallará en su propio partido una feroz interna para sucederlo.


El gobierno de Argentina también ve agravar sus dificultades. Apoyó a Bolsonaro que perdió las elecciones en Brasil y después se fugó con ayuda de Milei, creando un importante conflicto con el principal socio comercial de nuestro país. Ahora advierte que su mentor y sostén en Estados Unidos se ha convertido en un “pato rengo”, que ha perdido carisma y poder. Finalmente advierte que en las elecciones estadounidenses el voto joven se volcó mayoritariamente a la oposición y que este fenómeno ya está empezando a producirse en la Argentina.


Para finalizar y reducir un poco el triunfalismo que se ha apoderado de distintos sectores de la oposición en la Argentina, habría que recordar que en Estados Unidos tanto demócratas como republicanos comparten los siguientes acuerdos.


1. El gran enemigo a derrotar es China. Debilitar y tratar de cortar la expansión de esta nueva potencia emergente es la prioridad. El tiempo juega a favor de China que crece mucho más rápido que Estados Unidos, y que está armando una política de alianzas que pueden deteriorar la vigencia del dólar como moneda rectora de los intercambios internacionales. La guerra, que es cada vez más impopular en Estados Unidos y lo empieza a ser en Europa, se les presenta a las elites occidentales como la única forma de evitar la pérdida de la hegemonía mundial.


2. En el actual declive estadounidense, producto de las derrotas que están sufriendo en otros puntos del mundo, tanto republicanos como demócratas avalan la política de replegarse y hacerse fuerte en lo que considera su patio trasero (Nuestramérica). En la Argentina lo que no puede sostener Milei, lo intentarán con Patricia Bullrich, con Massa, Picheto o promoviendo a algún otro dirigente dentro del peronismo que se reporte a la Embajada. Por nuestra ubicación estratégica, en el extremo sur del continente; por nuestra capacidad de producir energía y alimentos; por nuestras reservas de agua potable y territorios con la posibilidad de instalar bases de big data; y porque es uno de pocos lugares del mundo que …

author: Maríangeles Guerrero
title: Las Tres Ecologías y la disputa por el espacio público en Rosario
content:
Por Laura Hintze


En la oferta gastronómica-cultural y del paisaje ribereño —por ahora accesible para todas y todos— en la costa de Rosario falta el Almacén de Las Tres Ecologías. Es un emprendimiento autogestivo donde, por más de una década, cooperativas, productores y organizaciones de la economía social de todo el país vendieron sus productos en un espacio público cedido a tal fin, en una zona codiciada por el negocio inmobiliario.

 Desde este año, por decisión unilateral de la Municipalidad, está cerrado.

 “El neoliberalismo es la práctica económica que, diciendo que está en contra del Estado, hace los mejores negocios con el Estado. Se apropia de sus recursos de infraestructura, de los recursos naturales o financieros para hacer negocios. Esto es lo que sucede. Es un proceso de profundización de la privatización”, reflexiona Roberto García, integrante de Las Tres Ecologías.


Durante años, quienes llegaban los fines de semana hasta el paseo ribereño podían encontrarse con un galpón de 25 metros por 10 donde había comidas, bebidas, artesanías, plantas, libros y textiles elaborados por cooperativas y organizaciones de distintas provincias

. Pero el Almacén no era solamente un lugar de venta. Aprovechaba su ubicación y el alcance a nuevos oídos y preguntas para abrir conversaciones a través de radios abiertas, presentaciones de libros, música en vivo, ferias y encuentros nacionales.

 Ese borde de la ciudad, a orillas del Paraná, se convertía en un lugar para producir, intercambiar y encontrarse.


El Almacén de las Tres Ecologías está cerrado desde enero. La Municipalidad de Rosario desocupó el galpón que había cedido once años antes a las organizaciones que lo gestionaban. Primero intentó hacerlo por la fuerza; después formalizó el cese del contrato por decreto. Desde entonces, quienes sostuvieron el proyecto se reorganizan fuera de ese espacio y buscan otro lugar en la ribera.

Detrás de esta disputa vuelve la pregunta que los rosarinos se hacen una y otra vez: ¿qué proyecto de ciudad se está construyendo frente al Paraná?


Foto: Las Tres Ecologías


El lujo es la organización comunitaria


El Almacén de las Tres Ecologías abrió sus puertas el 11 de febrero de 2015. “Ese día había muchísima alegría”, recuerda García. Habían trabajado todo ese verano para dejar el lugar a punto. El mobiliario, hecho con maderas recicladas, fue una de las marcas del espacio durante la década que funcionó: le daba un tono artesanal y luminoso que lo diferenciaba de lo que había alrededor. La inauguración reunió a amigos, organizaciones hermanas, ecologistas y autoridades municipales. “Fue el comienzo de una iniciativa única en todo el país”, resalta.


La apertura del comercio fue fruto de un acuerdo entre la Municipalidad de Rosario y tres redes de la economía social, solidaria y popular: la Red de Comercio Justo del Litoral, el Centro Ecuménico Poriajhú y la Cooperativa de Trabajo Encuentro Nacional. El Estado cedió a las organizaciones un espacio público sin cobrarles alquiler ni canon por su uso.


El galpón que recibió a las organizaciones cooperativas había pertenecido a empresas públicas vinculadas al puerto y al ferrocarril. Quedó abandonado después de las privatizaciones de los años 90. Según García,

mientras buena parte de esos espacios terminó destinada a proyectos inmobiliarios de lujo, otros quedaron en manos del Estado, municipal o provincial

. Ese fue el caso del galpón donde funcionó el Almacén, que quedó bajo la órbita de la secretaría de Economía Solidaria de la Municipalidad.


“La evaluación que hicimos hace 13 años fue que toda la costa se estaba privatizando y que solamente un galpón de 50 metros por 10 había quedado en manos de la Secretaría de Economía Solidaria. Entonces eso debía ser dedicado a prácticas relacionadas con la economía social y solidaria, una economía absolutamente emergente y débil frente a la economía de capital y del mercado. Nos pareció importante armar una propuesta en la que el municipio no hiciera algo estándar y llamara a licitación, que era lo que iba a hacer”, cuenta.


“Por eso no alcanza con decir que Las Tres Ecologías fue un proyecto cooperativo. Hubo una propuesta política muy fuerte: que estas organizaciones de la economía social, solidaria y popular pudieran gestionar un espacio del Estado de manera mancomunada, sin que el Estado aportara dinero ni les cobrara, sino que simplemente cediera el espacio.

Fue una experiencia de democracia participativa en el sentido más …

Bom dia, fim do mundo

Articulação dos Povos Indígenas do Brasil

author: Anikibawal
title: Festival MANOJO – INFANCIAS Y ARTES ESCÉNICAS. Una experiencia enfocada en la primera infancia donde se reúnen las artes escénicas, mediación y juego libre en la ciudad de Temuco este 6 y 7 de noviembre.
content:
Durante esta semana, los días viernes 6 y sabado 7 de noviembre, desde las 12:00 a las 19:00 hrs, se realizara la Primera Version del

Festival Manojo – Infancias y artes escénicas

, un festival enfocado en la primera infancia (de 0 a 7 años) el cual tendra lugar en el Museo Regional de la Araucanía, en especifico en el parque que alberga el lugar, conversamos con Brenda Lizama Farfán, psicóloga, bailarina de danza contemporánea y directora del Festival Manojo, quien nos cuenta en sus palabras

“Manojo es un festival de primeras infancias, dirigido también hacia esas edades, de 0 a 7 años y a sus cuidadores y cuidadoras, es una propuesta en el exterior, por lo tanto permite otras experiencias en relación a la exhibición de obras y a la apreciación de artes vivas.”


En su primera versión, el festival trae como impronta ser una de las primeras iniciativas de artes escénicas enfocadas de forma exclusiva en las primeras infancias, sus familias, cuidadores y cuidadoras en Temuco, entrelazando diversas disciplinas tales como la danza, circo contemporáneo, títeres y narración oral, junto con instalaciones de mediación y juego libre pensadas para la estimulación de las niñeces.


El festival desde su propuesta curatorial viene a buscar la recuperación de espacios naturales dentro de la comuna de Temuco principalmente, como lo es el Museo Regional de la Araucanía, desde la dirección del festival reflexionan respecto a “

el museo regional es un espacio que no abre por ejemplo, los domingos o que no abre después de las 5:30 hrs, donde sabemos que la mayoría de las personas trabajamos en ese horario, entonces, ¿En qué momento llevamos a nuestras niñeses a esos espacios? habitarlos, conocerlos explorando, y ¿De qué manera también les invitamos a explorar? ¿Pueden tocar lo que existe en ese lugar? Entonces, esas son las preguntas también que nos hicimos al momento de seleccionar este espacio para realizar nuestro festival”.


El festival cuenta con una parrilla programática qué incluye 6 obras de artes escénicas, a continuación Brenda, su directora, nos habla sobre las actividades y los fundamentos qué dieron vida al festival

“Manojo cuenta con una parrilla programática de 6 obras de artes escénicas, además contamos con una experiencia que es un laboratorio de exploración de juego y movimiento libre para bebés de entre 10 y 36 meses que se llama Danzas Sensibles, que es un proyecto que vengo investigando ya hace cuatro años aproximadamente, y además va a estar la Tribu Reverdecer de danza porteo, que también es un proyecto que da inicio también a toda esta propuesta de festival, fue mi primer trabajo después de ser madre. Desde ahí también vienen todas estas preguntas que les he comentado respecto a cómo las madres habitamos estos espacios: ¿dónde somos bienvenidas y dónde podemos criar en comunidad? Entonces, esta tribu fue un proyecto de acompañamiento psicocorporal y psicoemocional a madres, mujeres puerperas junto a sus bebés desde los 3 meses después del parto y desde ahí surge la danza en movimiento libre… , gracias también al poeta bebé nuestras piernas nuestros cuellos para poder danzar con nuestros bebés… eso también se va a presentar ese día del festival, somos nueve mujeres danzando con nuestros bebés. Creo que también es una propuesta reivindicadora de la maternidad, que visibiliza también a las madres, el puerperio, en un espacio y en un contexto territorial que muchas veces no es tan visto, no es tan visible y que creo que es muy importante tener ese gesto político dentro de este festival, que ya es una gran propuesta política que va a remover ciertas maneras de ver la danza en particular y también las artes escénicas y las artes vivas en el territorio»

, de esta forma, el festival invita a las niñeces, sus familias, cuidadores y cuidadoras, a pasar la tarde en el parque que antecede al Museo Regional de la Araucanía, incentivando a llevar alimentos para consumo propio y/o una manta qué permitan a las infancias ocupar los jardines del lugar.


Esta información se publicó en

Radio Kurruf

.

content:
El mal sigue aquí. 56 engendros, extorsionadores de mujeres, violadores, pedófilos y torturadores de la DINA-CNI, responsables de marcar a sus víctimas con cuchillos de combate, amarrarlos a rieles y tirarlos vivos al mar, de violar y abusar sexualmente, fueron liberados por la Kasta gobernante y están listos para reincidir.

En este thriller maldito, la Kasta está siendo coherente con sus siniestras convicciones y su maligna esencia blancona. Es la Chilean Horror Story, en la que calzan perfecto: dictadura, “Colonia Dignidad”, Paul Schäfer, Spiniak, “los coroneles” de la derecha, los decretos de libertad a criminales, y el alienado proyecto de ley de la escalofriante Vanessa Kaiser contra las víctimas.

Son crímenes inmortales de la continuación del horror político de “los nuevos padres fundadores” de los años 70 y 80, coordinados por el funesto subsecretario general de Pinochet, Jovino Novoa, el psicópata serial Paul Shäfer y los demonios de la DINA-CNI, que usaban como cuartel general de violaciones y otras torturas, la pedófila “Colonia Dignidad”.

No es casual que 20 años más tarde, en 2002, se inaugurara el siglo XXI con el sacrificio de niños y niñas de clases pobres, una nueva temporada de horror pedófilo por el mismo protagonista de la anterior, Jovino Novoa, esta vez acompañado por los libertinos vejadores Carlos Bombal de la Unión Demócrata Independiente y Nelson Ávila del Partido Radical; y dirigidos por el escatófilo Spiniak (pedófilo invitado).

El sacrificio fue quitada de cartelera informándose que Novoa, Bombal y Avila habrían sido “falsamente” acusados. Sin embargo, fue una generación que también en los años 90 albergó demonios torturadores y pedófilos organizados en el estado, especialmente los perturbados “Amigos de la Colonia Dignidad”. Algunos ya están muertos vivos como el asesinado, pero no menos maligno, ideólogo de la dictadura Jaime Guzmán; también, los “malditos Sergios”: dos ministros del interior de Pinochet, Sergio Onofre Jarpa y Sergio Fernández, y el grotesco delegado en la ONU, Sergio Diez. Y siguen vivos muchos “vampiros amigos” del Paul Schäfer” que traspasan siglos: Hernán Larraín Fernández, ministro de justicia y “derechos humanos” del piñerismo2 junto al conspirador Andrés Chadwick Piñera, ministro del interior de la misma masacre, el piñerismo2, ambos responsables de mutilaciones y violaciones a manifestantes del estallido.

Chadwick además, integra los “coroneles”, pilares del poder de los fundadores de la derecha, junto a Juan Antonio Coloma, quien fuese base “juvenil” de la dictadura, y también junto a Pablo Longueira, el mismo que habla con espectros. No hay que olvidar a las estrellas femeninas como la implacable -ya desaparecida- Mónica Madariaga, ministra de justicia y de educación de la dictadura, que dio el visto bueno a la constitución de Pinochet junto a Guzmán, ni debemos dejar fuera a la ambiciosa -y muy viva- Evelyn Matthei, reciente ex candidata presidencial, candidateándose otra vez, y defensora -solapada- de la criminal junta de gobierno, del golpe de estado y de la dictadura en que participó su padre. Todas y todos son villanos políticos, fríos y calculadores, además de grandes amigos de la pedófila “Colonia Dignidad” de Schäfer.

Nueva temporada: “La liberación”

La línea de la historia chilena del horror que continúan los padres fundadores-Generación Z, es innegable. En este inolvidable octubre 2026 de la Kasta, Fernando Rabat Celis, ministro de Justicia, Luis Silva Irarrazaval, vicepresidente del partido republicano y ahora ex subsecretario de Justicia, y Pablo Mira Hurtado, subsecretario subrogante, firmaron los decretos de liberación de sus engendros y mintieron diciendo que estaban “obligados” por una doctrina inexistente de la Corte Suprema, misma institución judicial que, apurada, mediante un fallo, los desmintió.

Ninguno de los criminales liberados por ellos había presentado individualmente un recurso de amparo porque los pedófilos están informados de sus derechos. author: CMI Argentina
title: Las políticas represivas desplegadas en 1000 días del gobierno de Milei
content:
El Monitor de respuestas represivas estatales o paraestatales a la protesta social en Argentina del IEF-CTAA presentó un informe que analiza en profundidad los datos vinculados a las represiones y detenciones registradas en todo el país desde el comienzo del gobierno de ultraderecha de Javier Milei.


La represión a la protesta contra la regresiva reforma laboral el 19 de febrero de 2026. Foto: Indymedia Argentina


Compartimos los puntos salientes del informe titulado “Argentina reprimida”, y al final del artículo, el PDF con el trabajo completo.


Informe del IEF: Los 1000 días de Milei


El balance de la política represiva sobre la protesta social bajo el Gobierno de Milei da cuenta de un uso intencionado, planificado y sostenido de la violencia como mecanismo de disciplinamiento social.


Los datos relevados por el Monitor de respuestas represivas de la CTA contabilizan al menos 147 represiones estatales a la protesta en todo el país, en las cuales intervinieron tanto fuerzas federales como provinciales con una fuerte presencia de represiones en la Ciudad Autónoma de Buenos Aires.


El conjunto de los eventos represivos analizados se reportan al menos 5141 personas heridas con distintos grados de gravedad. La evolución anual muestra un crecimiento sostenido toda la serie con un marcado incremento en los primeros 8 meses de 2026.


Entre los casos que a resaltar por su gravedad, se encuentran 6 personas que han perdido la visión de uno de sus ojos producto del uso de balas de goma y/o lanzagases en las siguientes protestas: Matías Aufieri, Ley Ómnibus, Congreso de la Nación, febrero de 2024; Claudio, en un reclamo de movimientos sociales por la entrega de alimentos, en la avenida 9 de Julio, en abril de 2024; Jonathan y Rodrigo, durante la protesta de hinchas y jubilados, en marzo de 2025; Marcelo, en una protesta de municipales de Hipólito Yrigoyen, Salta, agosto de 2025; y el caso de Lucas, quien perdió la vista de uno de sus ojos durante la protesta contra la reforma laboral el 11 de febrero de 2026.


Por último, se destaca el caso de Pablo Grillo, que aún no cuenta con una resolución judicial que determine los responsables que pusieron en juego su salud y su vida durante las jornadas del 12 de marzo de 2025.


La represión a los/as jubilados/as fue una política sostenida contra una población en situación de mayor vulnerabilidad, que reclama por sus ingresos y sus medicamentos. La agresión de las fuerzas de seguridad ha sido casi una constante en las protestas de los miércoles en el Congreso de la Nación, semana tras semana, con una presencia siempre desproporcionada de efectivos en relación con la cantidad de manifestantes.


Entre septiembre de 2024 y julio de 2026 se registraron 35 jornadas de represión a movilizaciones de jubilados y personas de la tercera edad, con un saldo acumulado de 1603 personas heridas y 164 detenidas.


Si se observan los casos de mayor cantidad de heridos en las represiones a las protestas de jubilados y jubiladas, vemos que en seis jornadas, ocurridas entre el 11 de septiembre de 2024 y el 28 de mayo de 2025, se concentran el 70% de las 1630 personas heridas.


En los 1000 días del Gobierno de Javier Milei se registraron al menos 762 personas detenidas por protestas y/o por estar organizadas. El 20 de diciembre de 2023, 10 días después de la asunción, se relevaron las primeras detenciones en el marco de una protesta social. Este tipo de hecho se repitió a lo largo de casi todos los meses en todo el país, con claros eventos de detenciones masivas en algunas protestas y un incremento sostenido de las detenciones totales durante el último año y medio.


Otro rasgo de los hechos de detención es que la amplia mayoría (78%) se desarrolló en el marco de 72 represiones a la protesta social.


En materia de la distribución geográfica de las detenciones, nuevamente existe una fuerte presencia en el territorio de la CABA, que es donde se desarrollaron los episodios más extensos y en donde se dieron detenciones masivas. En estos 1000 días fueron detenidas al menos 395 personas en 48 episodios.


En el resto del país, se registraron 367 detenciones en 19 provincias que ocurrieron en 77 eventos.


Otro dato saliente es el registro de casos de extensión en los tiempos de detención de manifestantes o militantes por participar de protestas o pertenecer a una organización popular. En este sentido, el Monitor de respuestas represivas registró al menos 13 casos de personas que fueron detenidas …

author: Administrador
title: Wir werden gehen. Ob sie es wollen oder nicht, wir werden gehen.  Denuncia der Gemeinschaftlichen Regierung der zwölf zapatistischen Caracoles.
content:
Musik: »Poblanas« der Gruppe La Surada. Sie sind Teil der Jarana-Gitarrist*innen (mehr als 40 Musiker*innen, die gemeinschaftlich spielen), welche beim »Konzert für eine Umarmung« im Metroplitan-Theater [in Mexiko-Stadt] am 18. November teilnehmen, wo auch Meme, Kevin Kaarl, Vivir Quintana, Ely Guerra und die Caifanes auftreten werden – um so die Kohle für den Transport der Familien Sucherinnen zusammenzubringen. Ticketmaster wird ebenfalls seine Gebühren für diesen Zweck übergeben. Aufnahmen, Zusammenstellung, Produktion: Terci@s Compas Zapatistas.

Wir werden gehen. Ob sie es wollen oder nicht, wir werden gehen. Denuncia der Gemeinschaftlichen Regierung der zwölf zapatistischen Caracoles.

Compañeras, Compañeros und Compañeroas.

Schwestern*Brüder, Schwestern und Brüder.

Dieses Jahr im Juli haben wir unsere Absicht bekanntgegeben, nach Mexiko-Stadt zu reisen, um uns mit den Gruppen, Kollektiven oder Gruppenlosen der Familien Sucherinnen zu treffen. Nicht für Vollversammlungen, nicht um neue Netzwerke und Koordinierungen zu schaffen, sondern um ihrer Geschichte und der Geschichte ihrer Vermissten zuzuhören: Gruppe für Gruppe, Familie für Familie. Und auch, wenn sie es akzeptieren, um ihnen eine Umarmung zu geben, welche die zapatistischen Gemeinschaften senden.

Wir haben Mexiko-Stadt als zentralen Ort benannt, um für Euch, die Familien mit Vermissten, Erschöpfung und Kosten zu vermeiden, die es bedeuten würde, bis zum zapatistischen Gebiet zu reisen.

Seitdem [der Ankündigung der Reise nach Mexiko-Stadt] haben die Bundesregierung, die Bundesstaatenregierung von Chiapas sowie verschiedene Landkreis-Regierungen eine Serie von Aktionen umgesetzt, die nicht nur die Menschenrechte verletzen (nicht nur die der Zapatistas, sondern auch der Partei-Anhänger*innen und Parteilosen), sie widersprechen auch der Rede von Frieden, Glücklichsein und Wohlergehen, welche die da oben predigen.

Wir geben Euch jetzt die Details; jedoch möchten wir Euch zuvor informieren: Diese Provokationen zwingen uns nicht, die Reise zu Ende November, den Aufenthalt in Mexiko-Stadt im Dezember sowie der ersten Januar-Woche, die sich konkretisierenden Besuche in Oaxaca, Veracruz, Puebla, Jalisco und Querétaro während dieses Zeitraums, abzusagen.

Somit müssen die da oben, auf Landes-, Bundesstaaten- und Landkreis-Ebenen begreifen, dass wir nach Mexiko-Stadt gehen werden (gut möglich, dass eine*r von uns bereits dort ist). Wir werden uns mit den Familien Sucherinnen, die das wollen und können, in Mexiko-Stadt, in Veracruz, Puebla, Jalisco, Oaxaca und Querétaro treffen. Wir werden der Geschichte ihres Schmerzes zuhören; wir werden sie umarmen; wir werden ihr Wort in unseren Web-Taschen [morraletas] bewahren; wir werden bei der Rückkehr ihre Geschichten mitbringen und werden sie bewahren, damit nicht das Vergessen und die Gleichgültigkeit sie beflecken.

Jegliche Provokation wird mit Entschiedenheit und Mobilisierung beantwortet werden. Sie müssen entscheiden, ob sie diese Tatsache akzeptieren und sich damit abfinden, dass wir unser Wort erfüllen werden. Oder sie können mit ihren Stumpfsinnigkeiten weiter fortfahren (darin sind das gesamte Kabinett der Bundesregierung, der Bundesstaatenregierung sowie Landkreis-Präsidenten involviert) – und [damit] unserer Initiative einen anderen Charakter geben. Wir wollen keinen Aufruhr machen, wir können es jedoch.

1.- Im Ejido La Culebra, offizieller Landkreis Ocosingo (regiert von der PVEM, der Grünen Ökologischen Partei Mexikos) fahren sie fort, Familien der [zapatistischen] Unterstützungsbasen zu schikanieren, zu bedrohen und einzuknasten. Diejenigen, die provozieren sind Mitglieder des Kartells von Mario Delgado, Staatsminister für öffentliche Bildung. Der Haupt-Auftragskiller ist Eusebio Cruz Ruiz, der sich als Lehrer präsentiert und sagt, er erhält von Mario Delgado direkte Anordnungen.

Nun haben sie einen Schritt weiter getan: Sie verbieten allen, in den Kooperativ-Laden der Compas zu gehen, ansonsten droht Gefängnisstrafe. Und auch jeder*jede Anwohner*in des Ejido und der nahen Gemeinden, welcher*welche die Gemeinschaftsklinik aufsucht (die Zapatistas, Partei-Anhänger*innen sowie Parteilose versorgt), wird eingesperrt und erhält eine Geldstrafe. Wer nicht gehorcht, wird inhaftiert.

title: Journalist Haşim Abak detained in Mardin
content:
Kurdish journalist Haşim Abak, a reporter for the Mezopotamya News Agency (MA), was detained on Tuesday night in the district of Nusaybin in Mardin province. Abak was traveling in a vehicle when he was stopped by police.


Necla Özgezer and a 16-year-old identified by the initials H. T. were also taken into custody alongside him. On Wednesday morning, the three were transferred to the Mardin Police Headquarters and handed over to the Counterterrorism Department (TEM).


They are expected to be questioned later in the day. No information has yet been provided regarding the reasons for their detention.

author: Bulatlat Contributors
title: Women on the frontlines defending land, life, and livelihood
content:
Across the Philippines, one of the world’s most disaster-prone countries, women are at the forefront of struggles to defend their communities against displacement, environmental destruction, and development aggression. From the mountains of Luzon to the coastal communities of the Visayas and Mindanao, they are fighting to protect the land and resources that make life possible.


Women tending the Kasibu barricades against large-scale mining


In Kasibu, Nueva Vizcaya, about 300 women are actively involved in a long-running struggle against large-scale mining. They help maintain six community barricades that have blocked mining operations since 2007. Among the companies seeking to operate in the area is North Luzon Mineral Resources Corporation (NLMRC), whose government-issued exploration permit covers 4,456 hectares of land, threatening farms and watersheds that sustain thousands of residents.

Click here to read their story.


Protecting the mangrove paradise in Tacloban


Further south, the struggle takes a different form. In Tacloban, elderly women are protecting the coastal community they rebuilt after super typhoon Yolanda (international name: Haiyan) in 2013. The typhoon destroyed most of the area’s two-hectare mangrove forest, reducing it to just 2,000 square meters. Two months after Yolanda, they joined other residents in growing seedlings and restoring the mangroves of Cancabato Bay. Over the past decade, their efforts have helped the forest recover beyond its pre-Yolanda coverage, providing habitat for marine life and a natural buffer against storm surges.


Now, that recovery faces another threat. The multi-billion-peso Tacloban Causeway Project is a 2.55-kilometer road embankment and reclamation project intended to connect the airport to downtown Tacloban. Residents and environmental advocates have raised concerns about its effects on Cancabato Bay, particularly on water circulation, marine life, and livelihood. 

Click here to read the rest of the story.


The women of Davao Oriental protecting Balete Bay 


Down south of the Philippines, in Balete Bay, Davao Oriental, women fisherfolk and farmers are confronting growing threats to the waters and land that sustain their livelihoods. Climate change, prolonged droughts, and rising sea temperatures are affecting fish catches and crops, making it harder for families to sustain their livelihoods. These challenges are compounded by the threat of large-scale mining in a province where around 80 percent of the land is covered by mining permit applications.

Read the rest of the story here

.


For the women of Kasibu, Tacloban, and Balete Bay, staying means knowing what is at stake when the land and resources their communities depend on are threatened. It affects how families earn a living and whether communities can continue to sustain themselves. 


Women often bear much of this burden, even as they take an active role in resisting the forces that threaten their homes and livelihoods. They know what it takes to stay because they have lived through these struggles and continue to fight for the right to shape their own future.

(AMU, RVO)

author: Kodao Productions
title: Groups vow to hound Trump when he visits the Philippines next week
content:
Fresh from his resounding defeat in the US midterm elections, President Donald Trump would not be getting sympathy from Filipino groups who promised to hound the leader they blame for worsening the Philippines’ worst economic crisis in decades.


Bagong Alyansang Makabayan (Bayan) and other groups and networks in the Philippines and abroad announced 12 days of protest starting this week against Trump’s visit to Manila on Nov. 16 and 17.


“Under the banner ‘Trump Out,’ we shall hold daily actions ranging from marches, rallies, indoor assemblies, public forums, pickets, concerts, teach-ins, camp-outs, and vigils aimed at expressing the Filipino people’s strong objection to Trump’s visit,” Bayan chairperson Teddy Casino said in the press conference on Wednesday.


Bayan said Trump will not come as a friend and has in fact caused untold hardships on the Filipino people and other peoples of the world.


Casino said they are raising many reasons to reject Trump’s visit for the 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits

 hosted by the Philippines that currently chairs the regional formation.


Bayan said Trump is accountable for the war of aggression in Iran, his support for Israel’s genocide in Gaza, military escalation in the Philippines and Asia Pacific, sanctions and military interventions in Venezuela, Cuba, the Caribbean, and the entire Western Hemisphere, his unjust crackdown on immigrants and critics on the US mainland, and his many other actions that harm the global economy and undermine world peace.


Trump’s real objective in the Philippines


Trump has made the Philippines as the US’ “first island chain of defense” against China and as a staging ground for military intervention in the region, dragging us ever closer to war with its biggest neighbor, Casino said.


The former Bayan Muna Representative recalled that in his last visit in 2017, Trump called the Philippines the most valuable piece of military real estate. “Since then, the US has drastically increased the presence of its troops, military facilities, and weapons systems all over the country,” Casino said.


Bayan said they are opposing the Pax Silica Economic Security Zone in Tarlac, a project Trump promotes as US’ “defense-industrial and dual-use backbone.”


“Pax Silica threatens to displace thousands of Ayta people and farmers, gobble up water and energy resources, and cause massive environmental problems not only in Tarlac but in mining areas all over the country. With US demands for extraterritorial authority and virtual control of our critical and rare earth minerals, it is shaping into a total sell-out of our national sovereignty and patrimony,” Casino said.


Nationwide protests


Bayan vowed to hound Trump from his hotel to Malacañang and everywhere else he goes while in the Philippines.


Bayan said various groups from Southern Tagalog and Central Luzon will converge with protesters in Manila in the run-up to Nov. 16. A big rally will be held in the afternoon of the 16th and possibly the morning of the 17th until Trump leaves.


“[The protests are] to remind him that he is not welcome here and should be kicked out,” Casino said.


Protests abroad


The International League of Peoples’ Struggle (ILPS) said its country chapters, members and allies are organizing solidarity actions against Trump’s visit to the Philippines and expected signing of the Pax Silica agreement with Philippine counterpart Ferdinand Marcos Jr.


ILPS said protest rallies, public forums, and other solidarity activities will be held in Melbourne and Sydney, Australia; Canada; Berlin, Germany; Hong Kong; New Delhi and West Bengal, India; Indonesia; Iwakuni, Japan; Malaysia; the Netherlands; Auckland, New Zealand; Pakistan; Thailand; London, United Kingdom; and the U.S. (Honolulu, Los Angeles, New York, Oregon, and Washington, DC).


“The actions that our members and allies are organizing in different countries are a show of international solidarity and a united front against the common and biggest enemy of the world’s peoples today: U.S. imperialism as represented by the war criminal Donald Trump,” said Azra Sayeed, ILPS General Secretary. #

(Raymund B. Villanueva)
